title: Festivals differ
hookLine: Vesak, Hanamatsuri, Saga Dawa: one birth, many calendars

lines: A BABY POINTING UP AND DOWN.
cards: A small shrine sits on a temple step, its roof covered in fresh flowers. Inside stands a statue of a baby, no taller than a teacup, one hand pointing up to the sky and one down to the earth.
A line of children waits with a bamboo ladle. One by one, each dips it in a bowl of sweet tea and pours it gently over the baby's head. Then they giggle and drink a little themselves.
It's a birthday party. The guest of honor was born a very long time ago.

teach.b: Why pour water on a baby statue? A Pali discourse, the Discourse on Wonderful and Marvelous Qualities, tells of the Buddha's birth: the newborn stands, takes seven steps, looks out over the quarters and speaks.
And two streams of water appear from the sky, one cool and one warm, to bathe him and his mother. The children with the ladle retell that moment with their hands. So the birth is shared.
First, Vesak, which you met back in year one, kept by Theravada communities in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia on a full moon in the month of Vesakha.
Theravada tradition marks three things on that one day: the birth, the awakening and the passing away. Lanterns, white clothes, temple visits, food given freely.
Second, Hanamatsuri, the flower festival, the scene you just heard. In Japan it honors the birth alone, the flowered shrine recalling the garden at Lumbini where tradition says he was born.
Korea, China and Vietnam keep their own birthday celebrations by their own calendars, with lanterns and the same bathing of the baby.
Third, Saga Dawa, a whole month of practice for Tibetan communities. Its full-moon day honors the awakening and the passing, and in some reckonings the birth as well.
People walk circuits around holy places, give to those in need, and some avoid eating meat for the month.
So the same birth may be celebrated on several days in one year, by communities that each have good reasons for their count.

how: Theravada Buddhists keep Vesak with temple visits, lanterns and giving; in Japan, Hanamatsuri is kept by pouring sweet tea over a baby Buddha statue in a flower-covered shrine; Tibetan Buddhists keep Saga Dawa as a month of practice, giving and circling holy places.

o: different days and customs honoring the same birth
rival claims about where the Buddha was really born
holidays each school borrowed from local harvest feasts

p: birth, awakening and passing on one day
a whole month of practice in Tibet
one cool, one warm, at the birth

s: the bathing of the baby Buddha recalls a scene in a Pali discourse
it tells of two streams of water, one cool and one warm, bathing the newborn and his mother.
all Buddhists celebrate the Buddha's birth on the same day
Vesak, Hanamatsuri and Saga Dawa follow different calendars.
Hanamatsuri honors the awakening and the passing too
in Japan, Hanamatsuri honors the birth; Vesak joins all three.

games.q: you're in Japan at a flower-covered shrine with a small baby Buddha inside. a bowl of sweet tea and a ladle sit beside it. what do people do?
o: leave the tea as an offering, untouched.
pour the tea gently over the baby's head.
drink the tea and walk away.
games.why: they bathe the statue with sweet tea, recalling the cool and warm streams that, in the text, bathed the newborn.

practice: Call up the little shrine of flowers and the children with the ladle. On each out-breath, picture a little water poured, one cool stream, one warm, over a birth you're grateful for: your own, a child's, a friend's, anyone's.

wordCard.voice: Festivals differ. Vesak, Hanamatsuri, Saga Dawa: different days, different customs, all honoring the same life. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Vesakha: the month whose full moon Theravada communities keep as Vesak.

carryVoice: Your line: one birth, many days. Nobody here is late to the party; they just keep different calendars. Until tomorrow.
